nodes.question: What type of abatement activity is discussed in relation to environmental protection in this paper?
nodes.answer: The paper considers the case of end-of-pipe abatement as an important category of environmental protection.
nodes.paragraph: Under cross-border profit shifting due to foreign ownership of environ- mental firms, non-cooperative governments have an incentive to weaken their environmental policies to prevent profit outflows. When environmental firms engage in imperfect competition, environmental poli- cies are used to increase the use of environmental goods. Furthermore, Sugiyama et al. (2023) consider the effect of environmental policies on the number of environmental firms. 7 See Greaker and Rosendahl (2008) and Sugiyama et al. (2023). An exception is David and Sinclair- Desgagn (2010) in which the simultaneous choice of taxes and subsidies is considered in a closed econ- omy setting. In a different context than that of this paper, Wan et al. (2018) examine the simultaneous choice of emission taxes and import tariffs when consumption of final goods reduces local pollution. 8 Following David and Sinclair-Desgagn (2010), this paper considers the case of end-of-pipe abate- ment. This abatement activity is an important category of environmental protection. For example, the share of Canadian industries expenditure on pollution abatement and control, which corresponds to end-of-pipe abatement, in air pollution management was 46.1% in 2021; see Capital and Operat- ing Expenditures on Pollution Prevention and Pollution Abatement and Control by Industry (Statistics Canada 2024).

nodes.question: How can an ecological tax help in reducing pollution and protecting the environment?
nodes.answer: An ecological tax can assist in reducing pollution and safeguarding the environment by encouraging the development of high-elimination and low-cost technologies, as mentioned by Tamara et al. This can effectively control carbon dioxide emissions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Ethical sourcing standards|Environmental protection measures_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What complex relationship does income have with environmental protection in wealthier countries?
nodes.answer: Higher-income individuals in wealthier countries are less likely to prioritize environmental protection, indicating a complex relationship.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract This study explores the influence of socioeconomic factors specifically income, educa- tion, and employment status on environmental protection preferences across 62 devel- oped and developing nations. Using a comprehensive dataset of over 78,0 respondents (World values survey Wave 7), we examine how variations in socioeconomic status shape environmental perceptions and pro-environmental behaviors. The results reveal that educa- tion is a consistently strong predictor of pro-environmental attitudes. At the same time, income shows a more complex relationship, with higher-income individuals in wealthier countries less likely to prioritize environmental protection. Contrary to previous research, urbanization is associated with slightly weaker environmental preferences, suggesting that economic pressures in urban areas may override sustainability concerns. Gender dif- ferences also emerged, with women displaying stronger pro-environmental preferences than men. These findings offer important theoretical contributions, challenging traditional assumptions about the Environmental Kuznets Curve and the role of urbanization in envi- ronmental awareness. The study also provides practical implications for policymakers, emphasizing the need for targeted environmental education and region-specific sustainabil- ity strategies. Keywords Socioeconomic status Environmental protection Environmental awareness Sustainability 1 Introduction Achieving sustainable development necessitates a holistic approach that harmonizes eco- nomic growth with environmental protection (United Nations, 2016).
